title: Significant Spatiotemporal Asymmetry in Future Global Rainstorm Flood Risk
content:
Abstract

Floods are among the most frequent and destructive natural disasters, yet future flood risk assessments have largely relied on precipitation indices, overlooking runoff depth—a variable that more directly captures flood hazard under diverse regional hydrological conditions. Moreover, the interactions among risk components (hazard, exposure, vulnerability) remain underexplored. Here we integrate 14 multidimensional sub-indicators, including both precipitation- and runoff-based indices, to assess global rainstorm flood risk from 1991 to 2100 under four SSP scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5). Comparative experiments reveal that omitting runoff depth systematically overestimates high-risk areas and brings forward the time at which risk projections begin to diverge across scenarios. Global risk increases persistently, with SSP5-8.5 showing the highest rise by 2100, and high-risk regions are concentrated in the Americas, Africa, South Asia, East Asia, and Southeast Asia. Exposure dominates risk, while hazard and vulnerability play regionally distinct modulating roles. Alarmingly, by 2100, half of the global population (up to 6 billion under SSP3-7.0) and half of global GDP (under SSP5-8.5) will face the highest risk level, with South and East Asia accounting for half of that population (or GDP) due to dense populations and infrastructure. This study advances flood risk assessment by reconciling hydrological complexity with socioeconomic pathways and highlights that mitigation strategies must prioritize emission reductions and the relocation of people and assets from flood-prone areas.
